In the second paragraph, after it says "Report" it says, "The unit is located from the 19th of September, 1992 in Dubravica-Krizancevo Selo in the elementary school." So could you please tell me, or rather tell the Court, did you talk to Darko Kraljevic in the elementary school of Dubravica in Krizancevo Selo or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I talked to Darko in the Kruscica hotel. I never went to the elementary school in Dubravica. Your Honours, until the present day I have no idea where this was. I do know where the Hotel Kruscica is because that is where I talked to Darko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is your conclusion, then, that this conversation was held before he moved to Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the conversation was certainly held before that, because it could not have been held anywhere else, because until the present day I do not know where this school in Dubravica is. So it is certain that it took place in the Hotel Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court whether you assumed the duty of acting head of the main staff of HOS for Bosnia before you actually received your appointment in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed the duties of acting chief, and Nedeljko, a man who was close to Dobroslav Paraga, told me that things were moving in that direction, that I would be taking over the command for Bosnia and Herzegovina after I went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And before that, did you take over from Jadranko Jandric this same post? Were you appointed acting commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by the very nature of things I took over because I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And when we sum all of this up, according to your present day estimate, when could this conversation between you and Darko Kraljevic, when could it have taken place, when you asked them to subordinate themselves to the Zenica command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This conversation could have taken place after the death of Mr. Blaz Kraljevic. It could have been the end of August or the beginning of September. Perhaps that is why Darko was so impudent, because he thought he would be in charge of the main staff for Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, this man called Nedeljko probably told him the same thing that he told me, so he was very arrogant towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We also talked about the number of Vitezovi, that is to say, soldiers of the special purposes unit of the HVO who called themselves the Vitezovi. Do you know anything about the Vitezovi, how many soldiers they had, what kind of unit it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to intelligence reports, I found out that the Vitezovi could amount more or less to one company. I cannot say exactly how many men they had, but the Vitezovi unit itself could have consisted of one company at the maximum, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know whether all members of HOS from Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez joined the Vitezovi, or only a small elite group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure, but I just know that Darko's unit was the PPN unit Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court the following: How many soldiers were there? How did this vary? For example, HOS, in its golden days in Bosnia, how many soldiers did it have and how many soldiers did it have before the April war of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the best of days the HOS had 10.000 men, approximately and in these difficult times, as tensions grew between the Croats and the Muslims, we could not even make up a single brigade in the entire territory of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My distinguished colleague the Prosecutor put it to you, and you confirmed that it was true, that a member of the Serb ethnic group was beaten up. And you said that was true and you said that this was done by Ismet Besirovic, a member of HOS. Please tell the Court what ethnic group did Ismet Besirovic belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officer Ismet Besirovic was of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You also confirmed, when the Prosecutor asked you, that there were some criminal offences that were committed within the HOS and you tried to deal with this. Was this fact typical of the HOS, or was it characteristic of other units too, or rather, of this general state of war in Zenica and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all the units on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, especially in Bosnia, had problems with such irresponsible individuals or groups of such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about crime in Zenica, did it go up radically in '92/'93 as compared to the prewar situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an enormous rise in the crime rate in this area, especially within Zenica itself. The state fell apart, the former Yugoslavia, and the system broke down. And perhaps this is too strong of a word but people went wild. They did all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, what about the man in the street? Would people feel unsafe in the streets of Zenica then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, no one felt safe in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And finally on this point, was this crime characteristic of certain ethnic groups or were there no boundaries in terms of the perpetrators and the victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regardless of nationalities, regardless of the units involved, there was crime across the board. That is the way criminals and thieves are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed your record of misdemeanours, 40 fights in which you disturbed the public order and peace. Realistically speaking now, after all this time, can you tell us whether you were involved in more than 40 fights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were considerably more than 40. There were people who provoked me to fight with them in a basement, at the Leveda Sports Centre, and I took them on. For ten years, I was the most physically fit person in Zenica, and various adventurers tried to provoke me, and I took up these challenges, and sometimes reports were sent to the police and sometimes there weren't. Sometimes the police would even congratulate me on this if I had beaten up some of these former criminals, but sometimes they would actually report me to the Court, and then I had to pay fines for these misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that, finally, you took all these tough guys from the street with you, made up a unit, and took them into the war with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. In a way, I was an institution that they respected, and they followed me into battle, and it is only such people who could go into the war at first. Other people faced a dilemma as to whether we would manage to survive or not or whether Yugoslavia would be in power again. These weaker ones did not take any actions, so it is only with these tough guys that I could start defending Croatian territories and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You say that you were an institution in its own right. You say that for ten years you were the strongest guy in Zenica. How do you explain the fact that you did not manage to subjugate Darko Kraljevic? How do you explain that? Was he as tough as you were on his own turf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, had this been in Zenica, I would have subjugated him. But Darko Kraljevic was an authority on the territory of Vitez, so I could not deal with such authority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put it to you and you confirmed that you even beat your own soldiers and officers every now and then. In your opinion, now that time has gone by, I mean, it's history now, in 1992 and 1993, was this a necessity in Bosnia? Is that the only way you could command a unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly, Your Honours, it was out of necessity. You had to be strong and capable and to exercise authority in such a way in order to be able to command such persons. Soft commanders could not lead a unit for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the state had broken up and you created an army, not only you personally but others, with guys from the street. What about orders appointing a person to a certain post? Was that sufficient in order to exercise true authority in terms of command or did one have to have other capabilities too in order to be truly in command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Orders on appointments were not all that important. It is local authority that was all important. So you had to look in the entire setup. If the local commanders wanted to listen, then things could have gone according to plan. If the local commander did not want to listen and if his unit wouldn't listen, then they wouldn't listen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina 3rd Corps. The deputy commander of the 3rd Corps was Dzemo Merdan, a very well-known person. Could you tell the Court the story, the anecdote, of one of your soldiers and Dzemo Merdan and a lamb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Above the village of Serici where, together with --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. President, this is beyond the scope of the cross-examination. We certainly didn't raise Dzemo Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, mention was made of command responsibility vis-a-vis Darko Kraljevic in HOS, and this is an anecdote which shows how important local commanders were, far more important than those who held higher positions. So it is not Dzemo Merdan himself who is important, but we should see how the chain of command functioned. And we did talk about the chain of command within HOS, so it has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please proceed. Put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So when they came into the hills where the Serbs held a line and then they had withdrawn to their reserve positions and these men from HOS had passed to there, Dzemo Merdan was there, this commander, and then these young men found some sheep. And they were driving these sheep, and Merdan asked one of the HOS guys whether he could give him a sheep. And he said, "Well, you go and walk around the hills yourself and get yourself a sheep of your own," and he said, "Who allowed you to go there?" He said, "Well, if Holman," he was referring to me, "says that we should go ahead, then we will go ahead, and I don't care who you are."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Dzemo Merdan say who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, oh, yes. He said, "Do you know who I am, the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps?" And he said, "Well, if Holman tells me to go ahead, I will go, but you can't give me any orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Finally, my last question, your opinion, you knew Darko Kraljevic. You knew the situation in Vitez. In your opinion, what about Colonel Blaskic, who was a former captain of the JNA and who was used to working the way he was taught at the military academy, who could not fight Darko Kraljevic, could he issue orders to Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A person like Blaskic could not order Darko Kraljevic. Local authorities were too strong, and Darko certainly held Vitez under his control. He held his soldiers under his control. The families of these soldiers lived there. So all of them were on the side of Darko Kraljevic. Darko Kraljevic was the most powerful person in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have thus concluded our questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Holman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There are a few points which I would like to understand more clearly, and I hope you can help me. Let us start by the order you received, the order of the Croatian Trefoil from President Tudjman. Was it customary that President Tudjman would give HVO officers decorations and some kind of gratification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot speak about what was usual and what wasn't, but I consider that for what I had done for Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think that I deserved an order of merit of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And this kind of order of merit would be given by the President of Croatia to people of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I got the decoration because I saved the young men from the former JNA who remained in the barracks when the war had already broken out from the former Yugoslav army, and I think that I did a lot to send the units to the critical points in Croatia. And I think that I deserved the decoration that I received and that it's normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would President Tudjman also promote officers? Did he promote Colonel Blaskic to General or promoted the others too or promoted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President Tudjman did not promote me. I received my rank from the HVO. I filled out a questionnaire in the main staff from the ministry in Mostar, the Defence Ministry in Mostar, and they gave me this rank according to the official duties that I performed. I was not given my rank by the President, Mr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned twice that HOS was -- first, you said that HOS was absorbed in the HVO, that was the translation I got, on the 23rd of August, 1992. And then you said again that on the 5th of April, '93, there was a merger between HOS and HVO. So when, really, did HOS become part of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are documents of the 5th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was the merger between the two? They became one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the army of BiH, we were within the composition of the BH army, and we were transformed into the armed force and another component into the Croatian Defence Council. Apart from the reasons I mentioned and the problems with the Muslims, there was another interesting point there. Because of poor coordination, these two components of the armed forces of the BH army and the HVO, and because of the poor coordination that existed, according to my view, we lost Komusina and Jajce precisely due to that lack of coordination. And that was one of the reasons why we decided to join the HVO, not to lose Croatian territory anymore, that is, that Croatian units should not lose Croatian territory under the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking, in fact, of not losing the Croatian territory, you mentioned that HOS believed that Croatia should spread all the way to the Drina. That's what you said. What would this cover? Which parts would this cover? Would this include all of the Lasva Valley, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This kind of propaganda came from the supreme command and the president of the Croatian Party of Rights, from Zagreb, and that included the Lasva River Valley. However, after this, the Croatian Party of Rights recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we defended equally both the Croat and Muslim territories. We defended them where it was strategically interesting for us to do so. So we defended all the territories, both by launching operations and defending the territory, as far as we were able, of course, because the Serbian army and the former Yugoslav People's Army was more powerful. They had already been organised. They were well-equipped. They had been trained for 50 years. We set aside our income, parts of our income, towards the army. And I remember when the Serbian units entered the village of Ravno, that the Muslims at that time in Sarajevo and in the presidency said, "It's not our war," but it was. In fact, it was our war because they attacked the village of Ravno and cleared it up, cleansed it, and that is where the Croats lived. We all lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it can't not be their war if we were suffering and just say that the war was where they were taking casualties. So that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, back to the merger between the HOS and the HVO, you said it was the 5th of April, '93, and before, on the 23rd of August, 1992, there was some kind of absorption. But whatever the date is, when HOS became part of the HVO, did it have autonomy in action or was it completely under the control of General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not completely under the control of Blaskic. Some units, for example, Kalesja, quite logically, Kalesja had to be under his control because the majority population is Muslim in the area. And Tuzla also relied on the BH army because the 2nd Corps was predominant there and strong there. So not all of them came under the command of General Blaskic. It depended where we were. If we were nearer to the HVO in an area controlled by the HVO, we would come under the HVO. And the units controlled by the army towards the Serbs belonged to them and defended, together with them, the frontline against the greater Serbian aggression. So let me say this again: Not all the territory came under the control of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in the territory where General Blaskic had command, would HOS be under his command? Would they obey him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There wasn't time to set this up. I understood subordination very clearly, and I would abide by it. Now, whether Robert Bresic, for example, in Maglaj followed these orders, I don't think he had time to. I don't think there was time for General Blaskic to establish this military and army system and hierarchy. There wasn't enough time to do this. So the area turned towards the Serbs was not able to be placed under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. Some were and some others were not. So not all of them were. I, myself, did place myself under that command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So people were free to place themselves under the command or not or was it a disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not a disciplined army. Once again, local commanders had their say, and they covered the terrain that they felt they were entitled to, and this was a detriment to us, the fact that we were not well-organised but, unfortunately, we were not well-organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you would still receive orders -- they would receive orders from General Blaskic. They might obey it or not obey it but he could give them orders or was it completely a parallel movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again let me state that Mr. Blaskic could not command these units. When I said that I would move over to the HVO, he was not able to command units in Kalesja or Tuzla because the BH army had them under its control, if you understand me, that area there, the upper area. So not everybody was under the command of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not the BiH, of course, yes. Thank you. Now, I want to ask you something concerning the misdemeanours which you committed and for which you were imprisoned. One of them was assaulting a public security official. That's a very important thing. Why did you do that? That was not a fight in the boxing field.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already explained this. It was the military security forces, and we kept the frontline at Serici at one time. I mentioned the young men and the sheep and all the rest of it. So at one point, we did hold these lines with the police forces and the line towards the Serbs. Now, why did I do that? I said that what I wanted to do was to save my men from the extremist units and their hold, for these units and MUP, because it was from these individuals that I expected to have more correct conduct, proper conduct. They knew the laws. They probably knew the Geneva Conventions and the rules governing warfare, and that is why I did this. It was an interesting point. This particular patrol passed into a sort of no-man's land where we did not have enough men, and so they could have had intelligence that we did not have enough men and not enough units to man this area. So those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm happy to notice that you mentioned the Geneva Convention, and you're aware of it. Apparently, some of your soldiers would sometimes commit offences against the Geneva Conventions. Would you beat them? Was there any incidents where you would beat them or punish them for offences, for any kind of crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said that when they beat up that particular individual and when I hit one of the men, I said that I did this to reduce and prevent incidents of this kind taking place, that is to say, that they should bring people in and beat them up. I wanted to prevent all violations of the codes of knighthood. I call this the codes of knighthood. I wanted to prevent individuals from breaking out in this way. Not all of the men were educated. They did not read much. They did not know what Geneva is and where Geneva is. They don't even know where Switzerland is. There were workers there, peasants, farmers, all types of people. I state once again that I relied on the MUP unit because they were more educated, but they too had amongst these units, wild units, catastrophic units, who didn't know about Switzerland or Geneva, let alone the Geneva Conventions and the codes of conduct in warfare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it recurred often, this incident that you mentioned. Were there many other similar incidents of people committing such actions without knowing, of course, that it is forbidden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, there were incidents of this kind in all the units, in the BH army, in the HVO, in the HOS, in the Patriotic League, everywhere. Incidents of this kind would occur everywhere. The structure of the population education-wise was not the same everywhere. There were people who were better educated and less well-educated and wanted to further their own interests. So people of this kind existed everywhere, and they had different motives. They had motives of personal interest and for personal gain, but I always liked the people who wanted to protect their family, their homes, their homeland, and so on, patriotic sentiments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You apparently tried to educate them. Did other people too try to educate them and prohibit such actions or punish them in HOS or in the HVO, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. I can say about HOS. Political activities, there were certain courses, and courses were held to talk about and discuss conduct, and we always asked our men to behave in the proper way. I think that this existed on the other side as well but, of course, what did the people know about what the Geneva Convention is and whether they all responded to courses of this kind to instruct the population and the men. Not everybody went to the battleground or to the units or to attend courses of this kind, educational and training courses. Everything was poorly organised because there was a lot of confusion everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Apart from the punishment which you gave which was a good beating, I'm sure you're strong, there were no other punishments, legal punishments, for those who committed crimes, apart from the beating, personal beating, to your knowledge, I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Would you clarify what you mean? What beatings? I didn't understand the question properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that you would beat a soldier who would commit a crime against the code of, what you said, the honour of humanity, crimes against humanity, because you knew the Geneva Convention and they did not know it. But apart from this personal punishment, because you were a champion and you could beat the others, was there any legal prosecution? Would they be punished legally or ordered legally not to do it? Was there any other punishment except you beating them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me try and explain. I didn't beat them up. I would give them one blow, so it wasn't actually beating them up. I thought that it was better for me to hit him once or to slap him once rather than having him beat up an individual and inflict heavy bodily harm. So I had to use methods of this kind. I had no choice, because otherwise I would be held responsible. HOS was an institution, and I was at the head of that institution, so I had to settle accounts in this way. I had no other choice. Justice could not cover the whole field. As I said, crime was on the rise enormously and justice just could not see to all these crimes. If there were more severe crimes being committed, we, of course, did cooperate with the legal authorities, with the law, as far as we were able. But of course we couldn't do so in all the cases, nor were we aware of all things going on, because there was general chaos and confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You understood my question, perhaps. You said justice could not be applied to everybody. But was there any legal action apart from the blows, your blows, was there any legal action against anybody for crimes committed, as you said, against what you called the Geneva Convention or crimes against civilians or crimes against humanity, legal action, or military action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any of the more serious perpetrators, with regard to crimes, criminal acts, as I said, I cooperated with the military prosecution of the 3rd Corps in Zenica. And if they were not able to do that with their own security forces, to take it further, then they would be taken to the municipal prosecutor's office in Zenica. I always tried to cooperate as much as I could with the security service centre, and I sent people to court, to the military courts, to answer for their acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there any punishments that you know of? Because apparently you were aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were some punishments, some of the men were sentenced, that is, they were punished, they got sentence terms. In my opinion, and as I see things, some of these sentences were deserved, others should have gotten more severe sentences but were left to go free. I noticed in this whole prosecution proceedings that a lot of sentences were under five years. What does that mean? It means that somebody sentenced to a term of imprisonment less than five years can defend himself while he is still free, he doesn't have to be in prison. And so, this meant that there would be more soldiers in the field, because they would be left outside prison, although his five-year sentence was still held true. And the municipal court of the 3rd Corps would later on take up this matter, and whether the sentence was ever fulfilled or not, I don't know. But many of these sentences were below a five-year term, if it was over five years, then of course they would be remanded in prison. That is what I know about the matter. I can't tell you any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I will just ask a last question to clarify the relationship between HOS and General Blaskic. Were there any clashes between some people of HOS, not you, perhaps, but others with General Blaskic, some open refusal of his orders, for instance, after the merger, when they became one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic could never control all HOS units. My units were headed by a local commander. I understood subordination, so he could exercise control over my units; but not Darko, Darko did whatever he wanted to do. There are various funny stories, I don't know if they are true, I heard about them from intelligence reports, that Darko would often do all sorts of things. If he really wanted to do something, he would simply do it. If he liked a weapon he would simply take it without the approval of the commander. That is why they were so well armed. For example, he would stop a truck and he would take the equipment and uniforms that he needed. So he didn't ask the commander for anything. I heard a thing which is sort of funny, I don't know if it's true, but that's what I've been told, and that is what I read in the intelligence reports: On one occasion he told to -- he said to General Blaskic at that time, he said, "Colonel, you have a nice Jeep. Why don't you give me this Jeep? If you have such a nice Jeep, I should have a nice one, too." Darko wanted to exercise his authority over things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You made it clear that Darko was what people would call "un enfant terrible" of HOS. But apart from him, were there others under the command of General Blaskic? Otherwise how would you say that HOS was merged with HVO? It was either two different groups or one. In other words, was General Blaskic the undisputed commander or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic could not have been the undisputed commander in any way. This was true in my own case, I realised that many units would simply get out of control, and there were quite a few of them. There were many units that refused orders to go to the line. "I am not interested in that area," for example, people would say that. And I, Mr. Blaskic and many other commanders could not establish their absolute chain of command in hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Holman, my impression is that the position you present is this: During an earlier phase the HOS was part of the ABiH, and then came the events at Dusina. And your appreciation of the situation changed, and then you moved across with your units in the HOS, over to the HVO side; is my understanding of your presentation correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I transferred on that date that this document shows, that is the 5th of April, and I put my unit and myself under the command of then Colonel, now General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, there were members of the HOS who were Croats and members of the HOS who were Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you gave the impression that the Croats were being victimised by the Muslims and that was why you decided to move across to the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the basic reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When you moved across with the units which you took with you, were there Muslims in those units which you took across with you from the ABiH side to the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims who were in the HOS stayed with us in the HOS unit. They did not leave. Those who were with us until the end. I pointed out before, before I made my decision, some of them left. Whenever an incident occurred somebody would leave, somebody would go to the Muslim side, somebody would go to the Croatian side; but they did not go to the BH army, these people who stayed to the end. Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kordic never said that these Muslims should be removed from the HOS unit. They never mentioned it. When I talked to Mr. Blaskic and when he told me, "Send your people to Kuber," he did not say, "Don't send Muslims, send Croats," he simply said, "Send your troops to Kuber," he did not say Croats, he did not say Muslims. So Mr. Blaskic or Mr. Kordic did not make any distinction between the two. They were good guys, they fought fairly and honestly, and they were with us until the end. I'm sorry if they are in trouble nowadays because they were with us in Croatian units, but for me they were good soldiers, they were crystal clear, they were good fighters and they stayed with us for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Holman, I was tempted to, but didn't, interrupt you as you spoke. If you would be so kind as to listen to my question, you may find it possible to give me a shorter answer. Now, when you moved across to the HVO side, did you find that you and your units were fighting against the ABiH or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not aware of the conflict being of wider proportions. In certain locations we realised there was a war between Croats and Muslims, but we could not realise that this kind of war was taking place all over. I only realised that later, in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't so much interested with the overall position as I was interested in the particular activities of your HOS units. Were they ever fighting against the ABiH or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HOS units that I had under my own control, under my own authority, did not fight against the Muslims. When I was being persecuted, when they were after me in the streets and in the hills, they even shot at me on several occasions, and my escorts and I returned fire on a few occasions because we could have gotten killed, but we did not wage war against the Muslims, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Against whom did you and your HOS units wage war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We fought in the areas of Maglaj, the most, and Seher, Serici, I already mentioned that, and we fought and we defended ourselves and we did not want the Serbs to take these Croatian and Muslim territories from us. We held the territory half and half with the Muslim forces. I already said that I helped Mr. Blaskic by sending units to Jajce and in other places. We were still oriented towards defending ourselves from the greater Serbian aggression, and that is where we were involved the most. We always sent our troops and weapons against the Serbs. Maglaj, Teslic, Tesanj, and even in prison they questioned me where my artillery was. And I said, "Why are you asking me that? You know I sent those artillery pieces to Maglaj to Commander Robert Bresic." Because Serbs were attacking Maglaj, I didn't need artillery in Zenica; so again, I was making it clear to them that nobody wanted to wage war against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you and your HOS units waged war only against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We waged war only against the Serbs. We didn't have enough time to fight anywhere else, and we didn't really wish to fight our allies of yesteryear, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When you and your units moved across to the HVO side, did the Muslim members of your HOS units know that you had moved across principally because of your perception that Muslims were victimising Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion a press conference was even held, that is to say, when HOS moved across to the HVO. We kept no secrets, and we thought that with this move we would be making a step in the right direction, that is to say, in this area where the Muslims were, where the 3rd Corps was, where they were predominant, we thought this was a step in the right direction, so they should not wage war against the Croats and we shouldn't fight against them. We still tried to save the situation to the best of our ability. We wanted to turn against the aggressors, real aggressors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You wouldn't say, would you, Witness, that when you moved across from the BiH side to the HVO side you were taking up the position that you and your HOS units would defend Croats against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to have a reconciliation in this way. I wish to repeat that. And at this press conference it was explained very precisely, perhaps there is even a recording of it, there was not a war against the Muslims. That Komusina and Jajce had fallen perhaps due to poor coordination. And in order to have greater security in Central Bosnia and to have a better organisation, it was explained very nicely that no one wanted to jeopardise the other party in any way. It was explained very nicely what the aim was. And also, we wanted to reduce tensions between Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question, time is going, it has to do with your conviction record, which I think is in BSC, and therefore, closed to me. You have seen the document, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean about my misdemeanours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, Witness, as to tell the Court which of these 45 misdemeanours carried the highest sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The highest sentence was six months, and I was given six months when I was going back home after my workout, and a friend of mine asked me to join him at the Phoenix Cafe for a drink. He ordered a beer, I ordered Coca-Cola with mineral water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you tell us very briefly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my highest sentence. This was a mass fight, many people took part in it, many people took part in it. Yes, it was a mass fight, and there were several -- several participants involved, and one of the participants suffered heavily bodily injury, I cannot remember exactly, a fracture or something. So this was the highest sentence I got, six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would I be understanding you correctly to mean this: Not that you had a bad temper, but you were strong and athletic and you sensed a need to act firmly to exercise leadership in very difficult circumstances? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, it was not that I wanted to impose myself as the strongest one. I really had these ideals. I wanted to defend myself and others from aggression, because that is something I had always wanted to do, even in these fights and these brawls. I always acted against aggressors. So I'm not saying that I really hit this man badly, but he did suffer an injury. So all of these were misdemeanours, really. And I would never attack a person who was defenceless. I observed fair play from the athletic field. If somebody would fall and if somebody could not defend himself, I would give up on fighting any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I only have one question to ask. How did the accused make his power felt? Was it through force, through his moral authority? Did he make his authority felt? Did he have authority? Did you recognise him as your chief? I suppose that the accused is not the type of person who would get involved in a fist fight in order to get his point across. In order to make himself understood or to get his way across, what would he do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying that we did not all have the same degree of awareness. I was aware of the fact that we needed better organisation of our units and I behaved accordingly. Had I not realised that, I probably would not have obeyed all orders, either. But I matured during the war. I first commanded a platoon and then a battalion, and I realised that someone who was a professional should be in charge, and not someone who exercised authority through force, that that kind of person should lead us, and that is on what our defence should be based. I realised that, but not everybody did, and that is why I listened to General Blaskic or I tried to listen to General Blaskic in this short period of time. But not everybody could realise that. Many still counted on force and that kind of authority, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Holman. We have finished, but not quite. Judge Riad would like to ask an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Holman, you just mentioned to my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, that there was no thought or idea of war against the Muslims. I just would like to know how we could reconcile this with things which just were mentioned today, here. One of them, you mentioned that the Croatian party was adamant to spread all the way to the Drina, and you said that it would cover the whole Lasva Valley. How could this happen without war? And then this came out that Muslims were cleansed from Prozor in October of '92, came into the discussion, so how could this be done without war? Is it logical with what you said, that no war was meant against the Muslims? Please give me a short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you were to look at the statute of the Croatian Party of Rights, and if you were to see what this party promoted, you would realise they promoted these objectives, or rather their attainment, together with the Muslims. You know what I mean? Including them, too. Croatians and Muslims together, that they should go all together, all the way up to the Drina River. I shall tell you one thing, I'm not a politician, it is hard for me to say this, but I will say this: There was some political adventurism too, there on the part of Dobroslav Paraga, and it wasn't quite clear what he intended to do with the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was their homeland too, you know. So I said this before the court of law during my trial, "Why did you go with the HVO? Why didn't you stay with the BH army?" That's what they asked me. And I said, "Gentlemen, the BH army and Paraga, who was in favour of the BH army, they never said what should be done with the Serbs." I shall just mention a figure, there was a million of them, and no reasonable people ever thought of harming them or taking away their lives or expelling them or whatever. So I did not understand this policy of Dobroslav Paraga that was waged from Zagreb. They said together with the Muslims to the Drina, but it was utopia for me. Jadranko Jandric, my predecessor, when I asked him why he was resigning, Jadranko Jandric said that for him that kind of policy is utopia, that it cannot be translated into reality. And I had similar thoughts on this. And what I liked was that all the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be constituent peoples, not to have any kind of sovereignty, absolute authority. In Yugoslavia you had that kind of thing. We wanted democracy. We wanted all three peoples to be recognised as constituent peoples. I'm not a politician, but I realise these things, I saw that something was wrong and that some things were pure utopia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I hope your wishes will come true. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People should live properly, everybody has the right to life; but also, those who committed atrocities and terrible things should be punished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are no further questions, I think we can now adjourn for 20 minutes. Thank you very much, Mr. Holman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the next witness brought in. I've got the summary. Therefore, we don't have to go through it. Simply say who it is, the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is Mrs. Zeljka Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we have her brought into the courtroom, please? I have a written resume in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please give us your name, your given name, your profession, your current address, and then you will take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Zeljka Rajic. I was born in Zenica. I lived in Zenica up until 1975. I got married and went to Lasva, and that's where I lived up until the war. I'm a housewife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your current residence, please, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At present, it is in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing as long as it takes to read the oath that the usher is going to give to you in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. You have agreed to come to testify in the trial initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor against the accused, General Blaskic, who is in this courtroom. You are a Defence witness. Therefore, the Defence will begin by asking you questions, the questions that it considers appropriate, and then it will be the turn of the Prosecution and then, of course, the Judges. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mrs. Rajic, good evening.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, that is to say, tell the Court, please, some -- give us some biographical data. You've already told us something. You said you were born in Zenica and that you lived in Zenica up until 1975 when you got married to the late Mr. Rajic, and you went to his village to live, the village of Lasva. Could you describe where Lasva is situated, how far it is from Zenica and how far from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Lasva is 20 kilometres away from Zenica and 20 kilometres away from Busovaca. It is practically in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So halfway between Busovaca and Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Lasva as a place, as a village, how many Muslims lived there before the war and how many Croats; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, up until the war, there were about 500 Muslims and about 60 Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you explain to the court something about your family? What did your family consist of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mean my family?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, your family members, you, your late husband, Mr. Rajic --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: And we have three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What are their names and how old were they when their father died?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Ankica was born in 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How old was she?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: She was 15 years old. Ankica was 16 years old, and Anto was 8 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court, please, up until the crime committed in Lasva, what did your husband do? How was he employed, and what property did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband was a transporter. He had his bus, he had a bus, and we were well-off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He was one of the richer people of Lasva, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You are a housewife. You say you're not a soldier. But as far as you know, is it correct to say that your husband was the commander of the local HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In Lasva, you mean.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your village, how many HVO soldiers were there commanded by your husband?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: About 30 soldiers, about 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, who chose him? Who elected him and why? Why was he elected commander?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, he was elected by his own people, chosen by his own people. He was chosen to be the commander, their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the course of this examination, we're going to mention two localities. One village is called Lasva and the other village is called Dusina. You lived in the village of Lasva; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the crime took place in Dusina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How far are these two villages apart from each other?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the local community, the municipality, called?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: It was called Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the Lasva municipality incorporate both Lasva and Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mrs. Rajic, tell the Trial Chamber, please, in this small village of yours, when did you, for the first time, become wary, to use the word wary, towards your Muslim neighbours? What happened to make you think about them?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was an incident with the Serbs. This was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: In 1992. And they encircled the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who encircled what village?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: The Muslims encircled a Serb village, and my husband was opposed to this. He went up to this Serb village and asked why this had happened, and he asked to be shown the order ordering this to be done. And as these Serbs had surrendered, they had surrendered, they had also surrendered their weapons, they had weapons, and they wanted to move away, and allegedly, they had Zvonko's telephone number, and they called him and asked him to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is Zvonko?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Zvonko is my husband. So they asked him to come up to the village and to bring another man, a neighbour, a Muslim, to come and collect the weapons and for the weapons to be taken to the local community. My husband went together with this man, they went by car, and they took this to the school, to the local community, and divided up these weapons amongst the Muslims and the Croats, the weapons that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And after the Serbs had voluntarily surrendered their weapons to the local community, which the Muslims and Croats divided up, what did they, the Muslims and others, do to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, once they had received weapons, several days elapsed, and they encircled their village. The Muslims encircled the Serbs, the Serb village which was called Bozici. They surrounded the village, formed an encirclement around it, and killed a pregnant woman. They killed her husband and beat up another man who died from the beating because they beat him with batons. After that, we saw that we could not have any trust in them. And when my husband intervened and asked why they were doing this, he was told, that is to say, this Muslim told him, I don't remember his name exactly, that the same thing would happen to him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what did the Serbs do then?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. After several days went by or two weeks, they all left, and they no longer live in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now we shall start speaking about the tragic events that occurred in Lasva and Dusina on the 25th and on the 26th of January, 1993. Tell us, did you have any information that your Muslim neighbours could possibly attack you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was some information that we would be attacked. My husband did not believe this. On that day, on the 25th, I asked him that I leave with the children because reports were coming in that they would attack us and kill all of us. He wouldn't allow me to do so. After that, a friend came and asked him, on his behalf, to let me go, and that's how I left. Around 2.00 p.m. on the 25th of January, we could not get anywhere because the weather was very bad. There was a lot of snow, so we spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: At Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So from Lasva, you came to Dusina, and you spent the night in that neighbouring village; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened on the next day, the 25th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: You mean the 26th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: In the morning on the 26th at 5.00, the Muslims attacked. We were shocked that morning. We only heard cries Allah-u-ekber, but we could not imagine that that was it. We were waiting for them to get closer. We went into the basement of a house, all of us together, the entire group, to see who these soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, the village of Dusina, was it attacked by anyone from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there an organised defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you see in the next moments? Would you please describe it to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I raced into the room. I called my husband. I told him --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you call your husband?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I telephoned him, he was at home, and I told him that we were under attack, and he was surprised. I said, "Zvonko, Dusina is surrounded, attacked. A young man was killed." He couldn't believe it. We left. Just as I got out of that room, a missile hit that house, and I went into the basement together with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers in the house who would offer any kind of resistance or were there only civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: There were no soldiers, only old men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Then what happened? Could you please explain this to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, when we saw, from the basement, that all of them were dressed in white, that they had green headbands on, and they kept shouting Allah-u-ekber all the time, we got out of the basement, and we held our hands up above our heads. Then they got very close to us. They grabbed our chests, and they threw us against the wall. They wanted to shoot us. They were intimidating us and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court what is it that you had around your neck?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: It is a cross. We wore rosaries around our necks. These are crosses with beads that we wear as necklaces, and we use it during prayers. So they tore all of them off, and they took us out to a clearing. They put the old men on one side and the younger people on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What conclusion did you come to afterwards? Why did they separate the younger people from the older people there in that clearing? What was the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that? Well, my husband had already gotten out to this quota, and they wanted us to be living shields for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A human shield, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean a human shield. They were shooting. They didn't let us lie down. They wanted to kill all of us, and they were saying that they wanted to burn the other houses. Afterwards, a neighbour came who said, and he was using a megaphone, he said that Zvonko, my husband, should go out and that they should negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute. Could you please explain to the Court where your husband was? He was on a hill nearby; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As the crow flies, what was the distance between you, the human shield, and your husband?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, about 50 metres, so it wasn't very far. And the Muslims who were behind us, also, they were about 20 metres away, something like that. And these Mujahedin were there. They wore beards. It was terrible. So they were standing there behind the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we move on to the negotiations between the Muslim who had the loudspeaker and your husband, tell me, who were the soldiers that you recognised there? Were some of your neighbours there with uniforms and weapons who lived near you before that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were there too, and then there were also some strangers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "strangers," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about people who are total strangers. As soon as I heard them shouting Allah-u-ekber, I was sure that they were Mujahedin. They couldn't speak our language, so these neighbours of ours showed them the sign of the cross, and that is how they knew who we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say that they couldn't talk, you're trying to say that they couldn't speak the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't speak Croatian or Bosnian because they are foreign people. And the man who did know how to speak our language, he used a loudspeaker to talk to my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what did your husband say? What did he want?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: He wanted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is "them"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: The Croats, the soldiers where my husband was, he wanted them to come down to surrender and to negotiate in Zenica. My husband did come down two or three times, down this hill, and their soldier who talked to my husband also went down into this valley, and they talked, the two of them. Then my husband went back up. And the last time, as he was going down, he had a white flag. Well, I don't know what it was. It was something white that he had tied to a stick, and they were all going to go to Zenica to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you said "something white on a stick," are you trying to say something that resembled a white flag that negotiators carry?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many Croat soldiers went to Zenica, and how many Muslim soldiers went to Zenica for the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: There were about 10 of our people and 20 of their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see your husband as he was leaving to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what happened to you after that? Could you explain it to the Court?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: After that, they took us back. Their head man, I imagine, took us to this village, and he wanted to show us to the locals. He wanted to show that we were prisoners, and there were also some amongst us who were wounded, and they laughed, and they said that all of us should be killed, that we were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who said that, your neighbours, the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, our Muslim neighbours, and they said that that would happen. They took us all back into a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And in this house --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, this house was in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Madam. How many Croats were there in this group with you? How many were detained, and could you tell me what their age was and what sex these prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a total of 30 Croats up there. As far as age is concerned, I mean, when you're talking about age, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking you who the youngest people were and who the oldest people were who were there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, I see. The youngest were 18-year-old soldiers and then all the way up to the age of 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And your 15-year-old daughter, was she with you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she was, but I was talking about the male sex. I was talking about the men who were there. But as far as children are concerned, the girls, they were from age 3 up to age 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So a total of 30 were in Dusina in this house. You were prisoners there, and then who came to this house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Serif Patkovic called Geler came to this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was he? What army did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: He belonged to the 7th Muslim Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did he say? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Patkovic had a notebook, all the lists of persons he was supposed to kill. He took people out one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the first name he called out? Could you please explain this to the Court? What was the first name he called out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: First, he killed my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I heard about it from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: When Patkovic came, I was sitting, and he said, "See, Zvonko took care of his family, and he left you to be killed by us." And a friend of mine, a lady, said, "That is not true. Zvonko did not take care of his family at all. His wife and child are here." He looked at me, he sat down, he sat on a table there, perhaps this was about half a metre away from me, and he said, "Mrs. Rajic, I can describe your husband now, what he's wearing." I was looking at him, and I really felt lost. I wondered why he was telling me all of this. He described my husband, that he had a helmet on his head, that he had a flak jacket on, that he had a Scorpio, that he had a camouflage jacket, like all other soldiers, and he said that he fired an entire round into his head and that afterwards they committed a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean over your husband's body?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant. They massacred my husband's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you believe it immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't believe it at first because I knew that they were going to Zenica to negotiate. Afterwards, when I saw that he was calling out the name of Augustin Rados to go out with him, and then a shot rang out, after that, two or three more shots, and then he would walk back into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. After he took Rados Augustin out, you heard a shot; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Patkovic come back on his own or with Rados Augustin?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Patkovic came back on his own. We didn't see Augustin after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So what did you conclude? What had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, we heard the shot, so we concluded that he had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now Patkovic, after having killed Augustin, he came back. Did he call out the next victim's name? Tell me, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, Patkovic would simply sit down. He would sit in a chair. He would start talking. He'd have a glass or two of brandy because there was some. He would have a bite to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you said he would have a bite to eat, what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, that meant that he was supposed to have a nibble or two while he was drinking, as if everything were just fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So he was talking to you in a friendly fashion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was talking to us in a friendly fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long did this friendly conversation go on?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: About 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what happened then? Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Again, he would take his notebook. He would look at it. He would call out somebody else's name. He would go out. Again, Patkovic would go out with this person. Again, we could hear a shot, one shot, and then two or three more, and then again, Patkovic would come back alone, and the same story. He would sit down. It was really like a provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As he was sitting with you, eating, drinking, you were wondering who the next one would be, whose name he would call out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us not burden the Court with dramatic stories, but tell me, how many times did Patkovic go into the house, kill people, and then come back into the house, talk to you, drink, eat?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Eight times, eight times. So he killed my husband too, and that was the ninth, and the tenth one was killed immediately. So eight times altogether he went out and went back in and called out people's names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And every time, did he make the same kind of break during which you would be expecting who would the next person be?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: The last person whose name he called out was Stipo Kegelj, a man who was terrified, he hid. And he said, "Stipo Kegelj, come out," and this man didn't come out. He repeated it twice, and he said that if he did not go out that he would kill all the rest of us. And the man was hiding practically in the flour. When he saw where he was hiding he started making fun of him. He talked to him a bit, "What are you scared of? Nothing will happen to you, come out with me." The man went out and he never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, these men who were killed, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, they were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what about Mladen Kegelj, what did you see in his case?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Mladen Kegelj was up to the age of 19. They made him undress and he stood there naked and barefoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And it was snowing at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was snowing. They tied his hands with a wire on the back, they beat him, tortured him, and they cut off his ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, what happened to the village, to the cattle, to the property and the houses, TV sets, stoves, VCRs, automobiles?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, as some were killing and torturing people, the others killed all the cattle, all the animals. Whatever valuables they could find, TV sets, VCRs, stoves, they carried all of that away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: These soldiers, you said that Serif Patkovic was from the 7th Muslim unit, did you see any insignia or did somebody tell you he was from the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: No, I saw the insignia, I saw Patkovic's insignia. It said the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So how did the killing stop? Why did it stop?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: It stopped, information came from Zenica saying that no one should be hurt in the slightest bit. But they didn't really observe that. That further enraged them, and they said, "Well, what did we come for then?" So again, they locked all of us up into a room, they were throwing some kind of fuel around the house, they wanted to set us on fire. And then Patkovic came back and said to me that I would be the cherry on the top. He ordered the other soldier to take me upstairs. The soldier came, and I didn't even dare look, it was terrible, all these people. As I was walking upstairs he said, "What about her? What do we do with her? Where do we take her?" And one of them said, "There's a room up here, get her into that room." And this other one, this friend of my late husband, former friend, said, "Don't, she has money, we will need her some more." I took the money out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And how much money did you have on you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: I had one hundred thousand German marks. And he said, "How much money do you have?" "I have one hundred thousand marks," I said, and he gave me 270 marks back. He said that I should take good care of this, that others would come just as they came and that they would finally kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After that, in the evening, around 8.00 p.m. they took you to the elementary school in Lasva; right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But before we move on to the other part, tell me, what happened to your property? What happened to the bus, your husband's bus? What happened to the automobile and all the things in your house?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: As we were going back towards Lasva, I met a man, a Muslim, a local Muslim who was driving my husband's car. It was a Siera Viberg (phoen), it was taken away immediately. The bus was torched, all the property they could take away they did. They took away the stove, the TV set, the VCR and 40.000 German marks, what I had hid in the chimney, they found that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You entered the school at about 8.00 in Lasva, and they held you there until the morning. After that which direction did you take?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Well, we went towards -- we went into the school building, and one gentleman asked that we be given a fruit juice or cigarettes and to have a rest, and we said the Ustashe would probably not get anything and that we would be killed as well. And the women said that, too. One man asked me where my husband was, and I wasn't fully conscious of the fact that this was done by Patkovic. Afterwards when we went down there a soldier crossed towards me and said, "Why are you looking at me? I didn't kill your husband." And then I became aware of the fact that he had killed everybody, and my husband, and this young man was frightened, as well, frightened of being accused of having done this deed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After going to the school, which direction did you take after that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: We went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And after going home?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: We went into one of our houses, that is my uncle's house, and they gave us some soldiers by way of protection. They said that nothing would happen to us, and they guarded us, and in the morning at 8.00 a.m. I went towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Madam, we're now going to hand around transcripts of the video cassette, and while this is being handed around, I asked you in preparation for this trial whether you would be capable of looking at the dead bodies of your husband and his friends, and you told me that you would be capable of this. Do you still say that you will be able to see pictures of this and to comment on them? May we show the videotape to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first part of the tape, it is difficult for me to describe it, but it is an atrocious tape. You are professionals, of course, but because of the viewers in the Court, if there is anybody who is at all queasy, perhaps they could leave the room, because it will be very short, very brief. May we have the lights dimmed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we have the translation, please? INTERPRETER: May we have a copy? May the interpreters have a copy of the text? "This is the body of Rajic Zvonko, Rajic Franjo, Kegelj Stipo." INTERPRETER: I'm afraid we don't have the text. "Kegelj Vinko, Kegelj Gragan, Ljubicic Pero, Stanisic Vojo, Kegelj Mladen and Rados Augustin. In the attacks by the Muslim aggressors army, they lost their lives in Lasva. May they rest in peace."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can stop, if you would prefer us to stop, Mrs. Rajic, do you want to rest a bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, there is no need for that, I can take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next picture is the picture of the lady's husband. Can we stop the tape here and rewind it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mrs. Rajic, is that your husband? What is this large hole here in the middle? What did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKA RAJIC
utterances.text: His heart was plucked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: INTERPRETER: "This is the body of Commander Rajic Zvonko. On the basis of statements, he was first shot at in the head with a Scorpio rifle, and then all these crimes were committed over him. You can see his heart has been plucked out, his hands have been cut off and everything else that you can see on the pictures. After this tape you will be able to see the people before this event had taken place, where the Muslim forces had set up barricades at Lasva, and you will see what the people have to say."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: INTERPRETER: "These are the barricades that were suddenly put up at the entrance of Lasva two days ago. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina units put up these barricades for no special reason or explanation, and that is the main reason why television Bosnia-Herzegovina paid a visit to Lasva, to find out why these barricades had been set up."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
